#4323. I finally got a USB-C charging e-bike, and it costs 75% less than Rivian’s bike

I’ve been waiting years for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging. We’ve already standardized much of our lives around the convenient little connector, from phones and laptops to tablets and countless other gadgets. But for some reason, electric bikes have largely missed the memo. Now, though, I’m finally riding an e-bike that charges with USB-C, and the best part is that it doesn’t cost an arm and a leg.

Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has quickly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a big difference.

When it debuted earlier this year, it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.

USB-C charging on electric bikes isn’t entirely new, but it’s surprisingly rare. Ampler was one of the first companies to introduce it barely a year ago, though its bikes are sadly no longer in production after the company’s bankruptcy. More recently, Rivian’s ALSO electric bike arrived with USB-C charging, but that bike costs around $4,500 – at least if you want the model that’s slowly starting to ship.

The ENGWE Zip, on the other hand, costs roughly a quarter as much as its only USB-charging competition. At €999, it’s priced at a relatively affordable US$1,100. That’s a quarter of the cost of the only other USB-C charging e-bike on the market.

Of course, it’s not nearly as technologically advanced as Rivian’s ALSO e-bike. But hey, it’s at least shipping.

And while the Zip is a fun little 16″ wheel folding electric bike in its own right, with a compact design that makes it easy to store and transport, it’s the charging setup that has me particularly excited.

Instead of keeping track of yet another proprietary charging brick, I can simply grab the USB-C charger from my laptop and plug it into the bike. There’s one in my living room by the couch. There’s one by my bed. There’s one in all of my friends’ places. There’s a USB-C charger everywhere.

If I’m traveling around, that means one less charger to pack. If I’m visiting someone, there’s a decent chance they already have a compatible charger sitting around.

Heck, I can even use a basic USB-C phone charger in a pinch. Sure, charging a relatively large e-bike battery at 20W isn’t going to be particularly quick, but the fact that I can do it at all is incredibly convenient.

Plus, the bike has one more trick. The battery also outputs USB-C, so I can charge my laptop or other devices from it as well. I can even charge two devices simultaneously, thanks to the dual USB-C ports.

The battery is housed in a roll-top bag that is locked into the headset of the bike but can be quickly unlocked for charging off the bike. And since it’s a keyed lock, no one can steal the battery even when the bag is left on the bike.

I typically charge the battery still mounted on the bike, though occasionally when I want to use a friend’s USB-C charger, I’ll just pop the bag off and bring it right up to wherever the closest USB-C charger is located.

It may not be the fastest charge, but it’s pretty darn convenient. And with a 360Wh battery, a powerful 100W laptop charger will still get it pretty much full in 4 hours, or for a more typical 50% recharge, roughly two hours.

And that’s really the beauty of USB-C charging. It’s not necessarily about charging faster. It’s about having options. It’s about not being stuck if the very specific charger that only works on your e-bike doesn’t happen to be around exactly where you are.

Of course, there’s a technical reason we haven’t seen USB-C charging spread across the e-bike industry quite as quickly as it has with smaller electronics. Most e-bike batteries operate at 36V or 48V nominal, meaning their charging voltages are higher than the 20V typically supplied by common USB-C laptop chargers. That requires additional voltage conversion and charging circuitry inside the bike or battery.

But clearly, it can be done. And if ENGWE can offer it on a €999 electric bike, there’s a pretty compelling argument that more manufacturers should be taking a serious look at the technology. In this case, it’s all housed inside the battery, meaning it could be directly incorporated into any e-bike whose manufacturer is brave enough to spec it.

I’m not suggesting that every e-bike needs to abandon its dedicated charger tomorrow. For larger batteries, high-powered chargers still make plenty of sense, especially when you want to get back on the road quickly.

But having USB-C as an additional charging option? That’s something I’d love to see become standard.

For years, we’ve seen how electric bikes are becoming more convenient, more practical, and better integrated into our everyday lives. Yet when it comes to charging, we’re still carrying around a collection of more or less proprietary chargers.

Now I’m riding a barely $1k electric bike that can charge from the same power brick as my laptop. And frankly, I think it’s about time the rest of the e-bike industry caught up!

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

Whether it’s the holidays, a birthday, or any occasion, we’ve got you covered with these editor-picked gift ideas for auto enthusiasts.

If you’re here, chances are you or someone on your gift list is a self-proclaimed car lover. Simple, right? No, not so much. Car lovers consist of different personalities and interests, and finding the right gift for your favorite one can be tricky. To complicate things further, each car enthusiast has their own favorite ride or style, making it challenging to find a one-size-fits-all gift.

We scoured the interweb (and our own collections) for the best car-adjacent goodies and discovered some fantastic gifts sure to bring a smile to any auto enthusiast’s face. Whether you’re shopping for a birthday, graduation, or the holiday season, here are the best gifts for car lovers, as selected by the editors of Car and Driver.

The Model T needs no introduction, as it is perhaps the most influential vehicle of all time. Your favorite car lover will enjoy building this Lego-fied Tin Lizzie, complete with white rubber tires, a gold grille, and a fabric folding roof. We tried out this RS2 kit, the Audi Quattro, and the 1990 Acura NSX, and were blown away by the quality. These aren’t knock-off buildable cars; they’re just as good, and their price points make them especially alluring.

#4321. Tesla Cybercab’s autonomy agreement is insane: $299/mo or it doesn’t move

Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested. The two-seater can’t move without a $299 monthly “Autonomy Subscription” that Tesla can reprice with a month’s notice, suspend for a week, or cut off entirely.

And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.

The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the company started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.

The key line is short: “Your Cybercab will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription.” There’s no steering wheel and no pedals, so that isn’t a figure of speech. Stop paying and you have a $30,000 object in your garage.

That personal-use clause kills the whole pitch. For years, Musk told people they’d buy a Tesla, add it to the fleet, and make money while they sleep. The first Tesla sold to consumers for unsupervised operation is contractually barred from doing exactly that.

Then there’s the geofence. Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas are already smaller in practice than advertised: when we tested them, real coverage was between 59% and 78% of the advertised maps, and parts of the Houston map have been called “fake” by the person tracking it. Now Tesla reserves the right to shrink that area after you’ve paid for the car.

Mark Valorian, who went through the terms on X, summed it up as “an endless variable-rate lease with a ridiculous down payment.” That’s about right.

Over five years, the car plus 59 paid months of subscription comes to $47,631 before insurance, registration, charging, and taxes, all of which are on the owner.

This is the part that should make every Tesla owner angry.

Tesla has spent the last year telling everyone that its Model Y is just as much a robotaxi as the Cybercab. Ahead of the Robotaxi launch in Austin, Musk said the cars were “the Model Ys we make currently, there’s no change to it.” On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call last month, AI chief Ashok Elluswamy said Cybercabs and Model Y robotaxis already run the same software, and that customer cars might join the network around Q2 2027. The Cybercab launches on the same AI4 computer found in the current Model Y.

So the hardware is the same, the software is the same, and unsupervised Model Ys are already operating in the exact geofences where Cybercab owners will be allowed to ride.

Yet the people who paid for it get nothing. Tesla started selling “Full Self-Driving Capability” in 2016 on the promise that every car it built had the hardware for it. Owners paid up to $15,000 for the package. In February, Tesla stopped selling it outright and moved to a $99 per month subscription, which still requires you to supervise the car at all times.

Tesla’s answer to all those owners is a new car. One with two seats, no controls, a geofence it can move whenever it wants, and a subscription that costs three times as much as FSD.

I’ll say it plainly: this car is for suckers who want to give their money to Elon Musk.

You don’t own a Cybercab in any meaningful sense. You pay $30,000 for the right to keep paying Tesla $299 a month, at a price Tesla can raise, in an area Tesla can shrink, under rules Tesla enforces, with a camera pointed at you the whole time.

There are three possible reasons Tesla isn't allowing model Y owners to use FSD in the allowed zones:

1: the robotaxis are in fact different from the model Ys being sold

2: Tesla doesn't have enough "remote operators" to cover all of those supposedly self-driving cars if users join the network

3: Tesla isn't willing to accept liability when FSD kills someone.

And the Model Y part is what gives the game away. If Tesla truly believed its unsupervised system was ready for customers, the obvious move would be to turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin who already paid for it. It’s the same computer and the same software in the same geofence. But that would mean honoring a promise made in 2016, on cars already sold, with no new revenue attached.

A new vehicle wipes that slate clean. No legacy FSD buyers, no HW3 baggage, just a fresh customer locked into a $299 monthly fee from day one. What Tesla built is a subscription with a $30,000 entry fee attached to it.

So what happens the first time Tesla emails Cybercab owners a month’s notice that the price is going to $399?

#4320. Tesla Opens Self-Driving Cybercab Orders To 'Select Customers' At $29,990

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Tesla will soon start selling its steering wheel-free Cybercab for personal use, the company announced on Friday.

The Cybercab will cost $29,990, undercutting the Model 3 by $7,000 and making the golden two-seater Tesla's cheapest vehicle ever. According to a screenshot of the order page shared by Tesla, deliveries will begin as soon as next month.

There are a few catches. The Cybercab won't operate anywhere in the country, Tesla says, but rather in "supported service areas." It will also require a $299-per-month autonomous driving subscription to operate, with the first month included for no charge. That totals to some $3,600 per year just to use the vehicle, before insurance or maintenance costs.

And the model will be sold to hand-picked buyers, at least to start. "Select customers are now being invited to purchase Cybercab for personal use," the company said in a tweet on its Robotaxi X account. Tesla said initial availability is limited.

It's not clear when or if sales will expand to the general public. But the sale of a car one can actually own that is capable of driving itself without supervision would be a massive milestone for both the automotive world and for Tesla in particular.

Putting autonomous cars in the hands of regular people has been one of Elon Musk's central promises for about a decade, and he's missed his self-imposed deadlines year after year. Meanwhile, today's driverless cars are owned and operated by companies running ride-hailing services, like Waymo, Zoox, and Tesla—not by individuals. The Cybercabs in operation today are part of Tesla's Robotaxi service, which opened for business last year and now shuttles riders around in a handful of U.S. cities, including Austin and Miami.

Tesla's biggest boosters online cheered the news. But it's also sure to tick off some of the many Tesla owners who have paid for Full Self-Driving over the years and have been waiting patiently for their Model 3s and Model Ys to become autonomous. Most recently, Musk said that will happen in the second quarter of next year in areas where the Robotaxi service operates.

The Tesla Cybercab has two seats and no steering wheel or pedals.

Tesla is far from the only company looking to sell autonomous cars to the public someday. Rivian plans to introduce lidar and a new in-house chip to the R2 in the hopes of giving it self-driving capability someday. General Motors plans to introduce an eyes-off version of Super Cruise to the Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028. It'll operate on highways first before expanding to other road types, GM says.

Tesla advertises the personally-owned Cybercab as "fully autonomous" and says owners will be able to monitor their vehicles and manage rides via the Tesla app. But overall, the announcement raises almost as many questions as it answers.

For example, there was no mention of whether customers would be able to add their cabs to the Robotaxi fleet and earn passive income, another longtime Musk promise. It's also not clear where the Cybercab will be able to operate, nor whether Tesla will expand that territory quickly enough to make buying one worthwhile beyond a handful of cities.

Another cloud of uncertainty looming over the Cybercab's rollout is regulatory in nature. The Cybercab's unconventional design has caught the attention of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, which questions how exactly Tesla determined that the vehicle complies with motor vehicle safety standards. The Tesla lacks a steering wheel, pedals, and side-view mirrors, all things that are typically required for a car to be street-legal.

The federal government lets companies apply to roll out noncompliant vehicles, but those deployments are capped at 2,500 vehicles per year. (Zoox, for its part, was recently granted an exemption to commercially deploy 5,000 of its autonomous pods over two years.) NHTSA has said it's working to streamline autonomous-vehicle rules, which could work in Tesla's favor here.

If Tesla can pull this off, it'll be one for the history books. Of course, the company has made numerous ambitious promises around self-driving cars—like 1 million robotaxis by 2020, and unsupervised self-driving pretty much every year since—and it has generally fallen short. Whether the Cybercab rollout breaks that streak is still to be determined.

#4319. Bit Reactor Exposes Clone Supremacy in Star Wars: Zero Company

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

For tactics titles, how you choose to build your squad says far more about you than any character creator ever could. With a genre so focused on how its myriad mechanics intertwine, it’s up to the developers to give every kind of player the tools they could want. Even so, stronger options will bleed through, building a toolset adored by the community.

Grand Theft Auto 6 is on everyone's radar, including the South Korean ratings board, which barely let it pass inspection.

In Star Wars: Zero Company’s case, developers Bit Reactor had some of the raddest sections of Star Wars’ mythos to pull on, tools they gladly toss straight to players. With that said, recently released community stats have showcased exactly how the player base liked to deal with the problems posed by the Infinite Coil: Total Clone Devastation.

Stat sheets like this one are always fun, showcasing how exactly the larger community picked their way through Zero Company and where they stumbled. For a black sheep like Zero Company, which came out of nowhere between other big-budget Star Wars titles, it swung far above its weight class, giving the larger gaming space tactics they haven’t played with since the last XCOM title.

Trick, the resident Clone in the playable roster, was by far the most popular pick, standing as the most deployed operator with a whopping 74.5% use case, followed by Cly the Mandalorian at only 55%. It’s clear that gaming fans still adore the Clone era of Star Wars, with Trick standing tall amidst his same-faced brothers.

Trick’s optional Bond with Hawks is almost the most popular in the game, really setting him up to be the fan favorite. It wasn’t just Operator stats explored, with the larger community whipping out over 226,056,072 battle droids, not counting elites or special variants.

With a genre so focused on how its myriad mechanics intertwine, it’s up to the developers to give every kind of player the tools they could want.

Standing high above the chaff, the Coil Enforcer beat the most players down, while Visser took his throne as the deadliest boss by far. He alone took down over 35,000 Operators, serving as a rather infamous difficulty spike. Through these foes, around 21% of the player base lost their first recruit, adding even greater stakes to the campaign’s end.

When it came to major choices, the community fell in line more often than not, with an overwhelming 97% hiring on Cly as soon as the opportunity presented itself. Hawks’ playstyle also seemed to coalesce for most, setting them up as a Heavy/Gunslinger DPS monster. With tactics like this, its no wonder the community tore through so many.

When it comes to games, Zero Company is doing wonders to keep Star Wars’ head above water after the hectic swirl of news surrounding Battlefront 3. Between it and Galactic Racer, fans are showing up for the smaller-scale Star Wars adventures, reminding the larger industry, as well as EA, that not every title needs to be some massive budget epic.

Star Wars as a setting has always benefitted from feeling truly lived in, and for an entire galaxy to exist, most days need to be occupied with smaller action. Pod Racing, tight tactical skirmishes, maybe some space wizards clashing behind the scenes. While the big releases are hotly anticipated, fans are more than willing to step into the shoes of smaller players.

Clones especially provide a really great niche for games, allowing players to hop right into a recognizable face without needing to give them crazy story significance. You can’t always play as a Skywalker, but you can always hop straight into the shoes of a Clone Trooper, even outside of their era. At the end of the day, every Star Wars game just needs to bring something new, and the tactics of Zero Company are perfect.

#4318. Huawei set to challenge Tesla Powerwall with new, 20 kW home battery

This high-tech Huawei home battery pack hopes to hold back Tesla’s latest Powerwall with silicon carbide technology, AI-powered energy management baked in, and enough modular storage to keep even large homes bright and warm when the rest of the block goes dark.

Huawei believes its new Luterra S2 is more than just a home backup battery. The Chinese tech firm is calling it an “all-in-one residential energy system” that combines a hybrid inverter, modular battery storage, and AI-powered energy management in a single, simple, and stackable package that’s available in single-phase versions that put out between 3 and 10 kW and three-phase versions that can push up to 20 kW.

The Luterra S2 is the first system of its kind to use Huawei’s proprietary full-silicon carbide (SiC) architecture, which promises improved efficiency, power density, and ease of use. It’s so easy, in fact, that Huawei claims it can be installed and commissioned in just minutes.

“We are thrilled to introduce Huawei Luterra S2, our next-generation all-in-one residential energy system,” said Steve Zhang, President of Huawei Distributed PV & BESS Business. “By combining full-SiC architecture, AI-driven energy management, and industry-leading safety, Luterra S2 is designed to be smaller, lighter, quieter, safer, smarter and more powerful than ever before.”

Huawei’s basic Luterra S2 configuration starts with “just” 5 kWh of battery energy storage and 3 kW of output. That’s enough to keep essential household appliances, lighting, and electronics running during a power outage, but you’ll want to keep going if you’re preparing for more than a day or two without power.

If that sounds like you, Luterra’s got you covered. The modular system can be expanded with modular 7 kWh LFP battery packs and can scaling up to a massive 336 kWh of total storage across interconnected systems, with inverter output peaking at an impressive 60 kW using three 20 kW units in parallel.

Keeping all that power cool and quiet is a Huawei-developed passive cooling system that does without external fans, keeping operating noise levels below a claimed 29 dB (about the same as my Mac mini). It operates at ambient temperatures from –25° C to about 60° C, and features a sturdy IP66-rated enclosure (safe to hit with a high-pressure hose) with corrosion protection up to C5-M to keep it from rusting away.

Nice, but no mention of price or European availability.

Alas, the Luterra S2 probably won’t be making its way to the US anytime soon – but fear not! If you’re shopping for a Tesla Powerwall alternative that won’t help fund the absolute worst people in politics, there are a number of great home battery systems on the market that can deliver backup power, store your solar energy, and keep your home running when the grid goes down. #4317. Honda Just Teased a New Hybrid SUV Called the Avancier

The revived nameplate is expected to debut in Thailand next month as Honda prepares a major expansion of its hybrid lineup.

Honda is reviving the Avancier name for what looks like a new SUV, as first reported by Automotive News, suggesting the model could play a role in the automaker’s renewed push into hybrids.

Honda posted teaser images of an all-new Avancier on some of its global social-media channels, showing a sharply styled vehicle with slim taillights connected by a full-width light bar. The company has not released any specifications, but the teaser confirms that the Avancier will be one of the first models to use Honda’s new-generation hybrid technology.

See all results for used Honda for sale near 98584

The Avancier name has been used twice before. Honda originally sold it in Japan as a wagon from 1999 to 2003, then revived the name in 2016 for a larger, more upscale Chinese-spec crossover. The new version appears to be headed in a different direction than either, with reports pointing to a three-row SUV slotting above the CR-V, though none of those details have been confirmed by Honda.

Thai media reports say the new Avancier will make its world debut at the Thailand International Motor Expo on December 1.

More important than the nameplate may be what’s under the hood. Honda announced last month that it would call its next-generation hybrid system “Honda Hybrid,” with global launches beginning in 2027. The automaker says it plans to introduce 15 next-generation hybrid models worldwide by the end of fiscal 2029, with North America a primary focus.

Honda says the new hybrid system is designed to cost more than 30 percent less than the system introduced in the 2023 Accord while improving fuel economy by more than 10 percent. The system uses a redesigned engine and hybrid drive unit and can be paired with a newly developed electric all-wheel-drive system.

That strategy represents a big shift for Honda. Like many other automakers, Honda had been pushing aggressively toward EVs, but changing market conditions have prompted it to put more development resources into hybrids. Honda plans to make all of its North American auto plants capable of building hybrid vehicles and expects to launch larger hybrid models in the region beginning in 2029.

Whether the Avancier will come to the United States remains unclear. Honda has not announced U.S. availability, and the company has previously indicated that some next-generation hybrids will be tailored to specific markets. For now, the Avancier appears to be an early look at the new direction of Honda’s global hybrid.

#4316. Diesel Prices Are Surging. This Electric Trucking Company Is Seeing More Interest

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

High gas prices have helped drive more interest in electric cars this year. But it’s not just everyday drivers who are looking to ditch fossil fuels.

Eye-watering diesel costs are pushing more shippers to consider a switch to electric trucks, Roozbeh Charli, CEO of electric and autonomous freight company Einride, told me in an interview.

“You’re definitely seeing an upswing in both customer conversations and just general narrative” around electrification, he said.

Diesel prices have risen far more severely than prices for regular gasoline, putting extra pressure on commercial operators. The average cost of diesel in the U.S. has shot up by more than 60% since the war with Iran began, to over $6 per gallon. Shippers are facing far higher fuel costs in Europe too. It all means customers who told Einride they’d revisit the idea of electric freight sometime down the line are deciding to get the ball rolling.

“A lot of those customers are coming back now, saying ‘let’s get started, rather sooner than later,’” Charli said.

There’s some evidence that those conversations are generating actual business. Einride, which was founded in 2016 and sells electric freight services and software, says its sales pipeline tripled year over year during the first half of 2026. Its conversion rate doubled over the same period.

And it isn’t the only one noticing an uptick in demand. In September, a coalition of shippers like PepsiCo placed an order for 2,500 electric trucks in a deal that’s set to double the U.S. fleet of electric Class 8 trucks. Catalyst Mobility, one of the nonprofits running the program, has said it’s noticed more interest in EV trucks from companies that weren’t involved in the deal due to diesel prices.

Charli chalks the increased interest up to a couple of things. The pricing pain today is part of it. It means there’s a broader range of customer use cases where electric trucks are price-competitive with, or cheaper than, using traditional big-rigs. Those are typically what he calls “middle-mile” applications of, say, 100-200 miles back and forth, with high utilization. That last part is key, since battery-powered trucks still tend to cost more than diesel ones.

The situation is also making some companies realize just how exposed they are to drastic swings in the price of diesel, Charli said.

Our weekly newsletter breaks down the biggest mobility news every Friday

The trend is encouraging for reasons beyond economics. Heavy-duty trucks make up a relatively small portion of the U.S. fleet, but they account for a disproportionate share of fuel consumption and harmful air pollution.

“Any exposure to diesel exhaust is going to be harmful to your health,” says Ray Minjares, heavy-duty vehicles program director at the International Council on Clean Transportation. “And so since there's really no safe level, the obvious solution, particularly in a world where commercial zero-emission vehicles are already available, is to switch to that technology.”

The Tesla Semi represents a "step-change" for electric trucking hardware in the U.S., Einride CEO Roozbeh Charli said.

High diesel prices aren’t the only tailwind helping to drive trucking electrification this year, Charli said. The long-awaited launch of the Tesla Semi not only helped bring more attention to electric trucking, but it also introduced a genuinely groundbreaking offering to the U.S. market, he said.

“The Tesla Semi, in a U.S. context, is definitely a step-change in the capabilities of the hardware” in terms of range, performance, and price, he said.

In August, Einride announced plans to deploy 500 Semis to service Amazon and other North American customers, tripling its fleet. Tesla’s truck is several years late to full-scale production. But given the diesel situation these days, maybe it’s right on time.

We all know the type: grizzled stubble, wraparound PitVipers, a MAGA hat quietly retired after last week’s deep-blue shellacking, and a pristine, polished pickup parked in the driveway that they “need for towing.” With Stellantis’ new patent for an AI-powered electric tow dolly that turns just about ANY vehicle into a capable tow rig, however, those might need a new to find a new excuse to keep that gas-guzzler.

Originally filed in 2023, Stellantis received US Patent No. 12,779,916 for its electric tow dolly on 03NOV2026. The patent covers a machine that’s designed to shoulder the trailer’s hitch load with its own ball hitch or fifth-wheel plate, using an on-board electric motor and battery to get the trailer going while its regenerative braking system and AI-backed steering and traction control system keeps everything pointed in the right direction.

In other words, the dolly takes on many of the jobs that traditionally require a big tow vehicle: providing the pulling power, managing the trailer’s weight and controlling its braking and traction. The vehicle up front doesn’t necessarily need a massive motor, heavy-duty suspension or oversized brakes. With a system like this, you could argue that the “tow vehicle” isn’t really a tow vehicle at all. It’s more of a “lead vehicle,” since the dolly is the one doing the towing … and it can follow just about anything – including the diminutive (and supremely affordable) Fiat 500e, which is also made by Stellantis.

To be clear, this isn’t just Uncle Jojo making fun of the commuter conveys – Stellantis’ patent describes the dolly as being equipped with an autonomous control system using cameras, sensors, a controller, and an advanced, four wheel steer-by-wire system. It also specifically discusses how the dolly’s independently powered acceleration, braking and steering, and sway controls essentially remove the need to own a truck in the first place.

The dolly system’s truck bed sides and small size allow users to experience the functionality and utility of a truck only when they need it, allowing them to own a smaller, cheaper, and more fuel efficient vehicle that suits daily use needs.

There are some pretty obvious practical questions still to answer, of course, including how much battery capacity the dolly would need, how much weight it could handle and how it would perform on long grades or in emergency braking situations. And, to be clear, a patent isn’t a product announcement or proof that Stellantis plans to put one of these things on sale – heck, if I were Stellantis’ CEO, I’d patent this thing just to prevent anyone else from building one so I could keep selling ancient, low-tech, high-margin Ram Trucks – but it’s a neat idea.

That is a funny picture with the tiny 500e "pulling" that huge trailer.

But on a more serious note, there's so much that goes into pulling. It's control. It's stopping. It's being smart enough to watch the weather forecast and know when to pull off the road and sit out a storm.

The irony here? Back in 2004, I began working at a dealership selling Chrysler, Dodge, Ram and Jeep. So of course we had the big trucks and many came in buying the 2500/3500 with the Cummins Diesel. Chrysler Corp made every sales person go through specialized training for the trucks and towing. Every sale had to include a form signed by the customer about towing and the limits of the truck they were buying. Hidden in there was a clause that stated the customer would NOT use the truck to tow more than the listed (legal) amount. If the customer didn't sign it, we were told by Chrysler that would be a no sale. They were very serious, and for good reason.

I may not like seeing all these huge trucks on the road. But when it comes to towing, mass is your friend. A powerful engine, huge (good) brakes and a well trained driver are a must.

I think it’s neat, anyway. What do you guys think? Are you ready to trade in your big-battery Chevy Silverado EV or Volvo VNR 800 on a new Topolino, or are you going to keep driving inefficient 99% of the time? Let us know, in the comments.

#4314. We Explored the Ford Vault, the New Home of Ford’s Heritage Fleet

From classics like the Model T to concept cars and race cars, the Vault is full of wonders.

Up until recently, Ford didn’t have an official collection of its many important historical vehicles. That all changed when Ford started curating its Heritage Fleet in 2024, and we got our first sneak peek at the collection in 2025. Now, however, Ford has moved the fleet into a new permanent home: the Ford Vault.

Situated in a nondescript building in Romulus, Michigan, the Ford Vault will house the Heritage Fleet, which includes everything from Model Ts and Mustang prototypes to race cars and one-off concepts. Currently, due to zoning laws, the building is only open to employees and offers limited opportunities for media, with the site formerly used as an Amazon warehouse.

However, Ford promises that it is working with the Romulus city government to get the building up to code so it can be turned into a public museum. The company didn’t provide a timeline for when the collection would open up to the public, but we got to take an early look at the fleet it has amassed.

See all results for used Ford for sale near 48912

Many of the cars were already part of the collection that we saw back in 2025, but Ford also brought in several new vehicles. We’re not going to cover any of the vehicles we wrote about back in 2025, so if you’re interested in what else Ford has in its Heritage Fleet, go check out that roundup below.

See More Cars from the Ford Heritage Fleet

Ford built more than 15 million Model Ts, but this one stands out for two reasons. For starters, this Model T was sold in the United Kingdom, meaning it has the steering wheel on the right. You’ll also notice that instead of the customary black paint job, this Model T wears a vibrant green hue. Henry Ford’s famous line of “any color, so long as it’s black” didn’t actually come into effect until 1914, once the groundbreaking assembly line was up and running. Before then, you could order the Model T in red, green, blue, and grey. Black paint dried faster, leading Ford to restrict the color palette once the assembly line was bustling for the sake of efficiency.

The Super Chief concept is the complete opposite of the bare-bones Model T. Designed as a vision for a luxury truck in an era when pickups were transitioning from workhorses to lifestyle vehicles, the concept took inspiration from the Super Chief locomotives of the 1950s for its domineering look. Under the hood, it used an innovative supercharged 6.8-liter V-10 called “Tri-Flex” because it could combust gasoline, E85, or hydrogen. Coach doors open to reveal a decadent cabin covered in brown leather, brushed aluminum, and American walnut wood. The glass roof sits over a structured grid of leather and wood, while the bed is lined with wood and strips of metal.

See all results for used Ford for sale near 48912

From the front, this may look like a normal Mustang GT350, but once you get to the rear, you’ll find that it has actually been converted into a pickup truck. This Mustang Ute project was built by apprentices in Ford’s metal shop at its Experimental Vehicles Building as a way to train them on the complexities of building concept cars. It uses the bed from a Ranger, and while it was never destined to be more than a training exercise, the Ute now has us daydreaming about a hi-po successor to the Falcon Ute sold in Australia until 2016.

The Model T isn’t the only foreign-market car in the collection. This is the adorable first-generation Ka, a tiny hatchback sold in Europe from 1996 to 2008. In fact, this was the final first-gen Ka to roll off the production line, and it has fewer than 10 miles on the odometer, making it probably the most pristine Ka in existence. The Ka was a big success for Ford, and it even spawned a convertible called the StreetKa, which we’d love to see added to the collection in the future.

Ford has called its upcoming Fathom electric truck a “Model T moment,” but this isn’t the first time the company has employed such language. The 2003 Model U concept was designed as a modern take on the Model T’s “people’s car” approach. It was a small pickup truck that could be transformed into an SUV via a retractable rear section. It also had a retractable canvas roof and exterior body panels made from a soy-based material. Under the hood lived a supercharged 2.3-liter four-cylinder hydrogen-combustion engine mated to an electrified automatic transmission. The Model U got a claimed 45 mpg and was loaded with features that weren’t yet common in 2003, from a head-up display to adaptive headlights and automatic emergency braking.

The Ford Bronco was killed off in 1996, but by 1999 there were already plans to bring the off-roader back. Designer Moray Callum led a team that proposed this next-generation Bronco, known under the codename U260. It was based on a Ranger platform, but never progressed much beyond this exterior-styling prototype. Ford would revisit the Bronco in 2004 with a concept that debuted at the Detroit auto show, which also lives in the Heritage Fleet, but we’d have to wait until 2021 to see the Bronco name return on a production car.

Love it or hate it, the SYNus is certainly one of the most unique-looking vehicles to ever wear the Blue Oval. While it looks like it should be pronounced like “sinus,” the name is actually meant to be said “sin-you-ehs,” combining “synthesis” and US, standing for “Urban Sanctuary.” The design looks like a bank vault on wheels, with thin windows, slab-sided bodywork, and even a wheel handle for the rear door. While it looks imposing in photos, the SYNus is actually quite small in person, only measuring 158 inches long. It was powered by a 134-hp 2.0-liter four-cylinder mated to a five-speed manual.

These days, Lincoln only sells SUVs, but back in the ’90s, the luxury division considered building a two-door roadster. The L2K began as a proposal for a Mercury sports car, before Ford brass changed their mind. Built on a heavily modified chassis from a 1993 Mazda Miata, the L2K packed a 250-hp 3.4-liter V-8 engine and a four-speed automatic. The L2K was a drivable concept, and it reportedly completed around 100 laps of Saugus Speedway in Santa Clarita, California. It then debuted at the Los Angeles auto show and toured the show circuit before management scrapped the project. While there were reports that the L2K was scrapped, the slinky Lincoln clearly survived.

This pointy concept from 1963 is actually based on a Shelby Cobra, eschewing the iconic curvaceous body for a wedge shape. Designed by Eugene Bordinat, Ford’s head of styling at the time, the Cougar II’s fastback fiberglass body looks sleek and modern, with a rich red paint job accented by chrome trim. The Cougar II also wore pop-up headlights, and improved aerodynamics meant it could allegedly hit 170 mph (10 more than a standard 260 V-8-powered Cobra). The Cougar II and a similar concept, the Bordinat Cobra, are on loan from the Detroit Historical Society, and the Ford Vault may include more vehicles on loan for rotating exhibits once it opens to the public.

Many of Ford’s concept cars feature experimental powertrains, and the Reflex is no exception. This futuristic-looking compact coupe was motivated by a diesel-electric hybrid engine with innovative-for-the-time lithium-ion batteries. Ford claims the Reflex could return 65 mpg, and with an electric motor on the rear axle providing all-wheel drive, 60 mph arrived in a claimed 7.0 seconds. Opening the rear-hinged butterfly doors reveals a cabin that looks inspired by athletic wear, with lightweight seats upholstered in mesh and rubber in the floor taken from Nike shoes. The Reflex also has a 2+1 layout, with a single “love seat” mounted behind the front passengers, along with an integrated child seat and a baby camera monitor mounted in the dash. Sadly, this mixture of sporty and practical never made it into production.

We’ll close with a trio of vehicles that won’t be in the Vault beyond the next few days, but are too good to not include. These are the three Ford GT40 race cars that, somewhat controversially, crossed the finish line together to take the top three spots at the 1966 24 Hours of Le Mans. The legendary finish saw the black No. 2 Shelby American car driven by Bruce McLaren take first place ahead of Ken Miles in the blue-and-red No. 2, who had been leading for much of the race’s final hours and had been asked to slow so that the three leading GT40s could finish together.

Caleb Miller began blogging about cars at 13 years old, and he realized his dream of writing for a car magazine after graduating from Carnegie Mellon University and joining the Car and Driver team. He loves quirky and obscure autos, aiming to one day own something bizarre like a Nissan S-Cargo, and is an avid motorsports fan.

#4313. $20K Nissan NX7 PHEV goes on sale with nearly 200 miles of electric range

Dongfeng Nissan officially opened the early order book on its new NX7 hybrid yesterday, promising up to 320 km (~198 miles) of all-electric range from a 40 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery and a $20,000 price tag.

When the first generation Nissan LEAF bowed with 70-ish miles of range from its 24 kWh li-ion battery pack, it struggled to meet widespread adoption, especially in an SUV-obsessed US market that demands forethought-free trips to Home Depot and bladder-busting range. The company’s latest 2027 Rogue Hybrid is a step in the right direction, using a gas engine to generate electricity for a pair of electric drive motors that deliver a driving experience that’s remarkably similar to a “pure” electric car – but without a plug, it’s still entirely dependent on fossil fuels. The new Dongfeng Nissan NX7, though? That’s a different story.

The plug-in hybrid Dongfeng Nissan NX7 might be called a “long range hybrid” in the same sense that Volvo’s Euro-market XC70 is, in that it’s an EV for the 360-odd days a year that you’re driving less than 200 miles, and an ICE vehicle for the handful of days you drive more. And if you’re one of those people who thinks stopping on road trips is a character flaw, a fully charged and topped off NX7 will take you an astonishing 1,666 km (~1,035 miles) from where you started.

The new NX7 could be an ideal lilypad vehicle for North American drivers who are either too afraid of being caught without a charger or too invested in the outcome of one or more dumb oil wars to confidently make the switch to EV – and, even at twice the 129,900 yuan ($~19,400) asking price, I think it would be a hit.

For that money, NX7 buyers get an absolutely loaded Model Y-sized crossover (they’re within 1/4″ of each other in length), with a 17.3″ central touchscreen, a fully digital instrument cluster, and (on higher-spec models) a positively massive 55″ augmented-reality head-up display powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8295P automotive processor and running on Nissan OS 3.0 with an AI-powered voice assistant developed with iFlytek that, Nissan claims, can recognize natural-language commands, remember user preferences, and even recognize occupants, adjusting vehicle settings accordingly.

On top-shelf models, the NX7 cabins get “AI Zero-Pressure Cloud Blanket” seats that use sensors and air-cushion arrays to dynamically adjust for maximum comfort, and include heating, ventilation, and a 12-point SPA-level massage function. The front seats can be fully reclined to create a bed-like configuration that will be familiar to Cube owners. The NX7 even offers an on-board refrigerator and motion-sickness prevention system that Nissan claims can reduce motion sickness by as much as 83% (which, like, I wouldn’t want to be the one to test that – but seems cool).

Power comes from a 1.5-liter naturally aspirated internal combustion engine making 98 hp that’s paired to a 228 hp electric drive motor and the previously mentioned 40.9 kWh LFP battery. It’s not immediately clear if the NX7 uses a conventional parallel hybrid system like a Prius or a series-hybrid-plus-plug setup, but Dongfeng’s hybrid technology patents describe a pretty versatile arrangement with four possible operating modes: series hybrid, parallel hybrid, direct engine drive and electricity generation – which means the vehicle can theoretically use the ICE motor as a generator, drive the wheels mechanically, or work alongside the electric motor, depending on what the operating conditions call for. Whether any or all four modes make it to production on the NX7 remains to be seen, but it’s an intriguing bit of engineering for a vehicle promising nearly 200 miles of electric driving range.

The final production version will be shown to the public for the first time at the Guangzhou Auto Show later this month, but you can let us know what you think of the new NX7 in the comments, today.

SOURCE | IMAGES: Dongfeng Nissan, via CarNewsChina.

#4312. Comparison Test: 2026 Jeep Recon Moab vs. 2027 Rivian R2 Performance

Two squared-off electric SUVs square off.

Normally, it’s easy to identify an incumbent. Establishment figures tend to enjoy advantages—experience, name recognition, resources—that are scarce for upstarts. But in the case of the 2027 Rivian R2 and the 2026 Jeep Recon Moab, it’s hard to say who’s the incumbent and who’s the challenger. Jeep has been building SUVs since the 1940s, as it’s happy to constantly remind you, but is relatively new to EVs. Meanwhile, the first Rivians hit the road just five years ago, but EVs are all that it builds, and the R2 is the brand’s third model. Which incumbency is more advantageous? Let’s take a look.

The fresh-out-of-the-oven R2 hews to the typical launch strategy of offering the most expensive version first. Thus, our 2027 model is a Performance trim with the Launch package, which brings a 4400-pound tow rating and hands-free driving assist. Simpler variants are coming soon, priced closer to 50 grand, but our tester with its $2000 Launch Green paint tallied $61,485. Happily, the R2’s most delightful feature, its power roll-down hatch glass, is standard. Sorry, Toyota 4Runner, Rivian is onto the lifestyle appeal of a dropped rear window with a surfboard poking out. Or a dog or two who won’t be breathing exhaust fumes.

See all results for new 2026 Jeep Recon EV for sale near 08060

The Recon is so far only available in Moab trim, which at Jeep signifies elevated off-road capability along with an elevated price. Indeed, the Recon’s $68,990 base sticker exceeds the R2’s as-tested figure, and an assortment of goodies further inflated our as-tested price to $73,345. Major options included the $1995 Comfort package, which adds ventilated front seats and heated second-row seats, and the $995 towing package (max capacity: 3300 pounds). Plenty of off-road hardware is standard: skid plates, an electronically locking rear differential, and 33-inch all-terrain tires. And because Jeep is leaning into the “Wrangler, but electric” theme, the Recon’s doors and rear windows are removable without tools. But, at about 70 pounds each, the doors might not be removable without a daily swig of creatine.

The R2’s styling is “Honey, I Shrunk the R1.” It’s clean, modern, and employs the signature Rivian ovoid headlights. There’s nothing too revolutionary about it, but that works to its advantage—Rivian wants to sell the hell out of this thing, and divisive styling is not a smart play for conquesting market share from internal-combustion rivals. (Just ask the Tesla Cybertruck.) And, hey, you can’t go wrong with big wheels pushed out to the corners. Our tester had all-season tires on 21-inch wheels, the mall-crawler spec, but Rivian does offer tougher-looking 20-inch wheels with all-terrain tires. Those, however, will drop EPA-rated range from 330 miles to 307 miles.

See all results for new 2026 Jeep Recon EV for sale near 08060

The Recon’s aesthetic is intentionally anti-EV, with nary a concession to aerodynamics or rolling resistance. It’s square, tall, and has a front bumper that looks like a bulldog’s underbite, all of which contributes to an atmosphere-battling 0.404 coefficient of drag. It doesn’t quite pull off the Wrangler’s studied minimalism, but the Recon is the most off-road-forward EV this side of a Hummer or a Mercedes-Benz G580e. It’s also capable of changing up its look, depending on whether the doors and windows are removed. Buttoned up, it’s a regular SUV with an off-road bent, but ditch the doors and open the full-length canvas roof, and it’s like you’re driving something from the car-stripping contest in I’m Gonna Git You Sucka.

Inside, the R2 and Recon represent their respective manufacturers’ design philosophies. Whether you prefer the spare, screen-centric Rivian or the more conventional Jeep is a matter of your priorities (and, maybe, age), but the Recon is undeniably more user-friendly. Stellantis may whipsaw on its product planning—EVs! No, V-8s!—but its interiors are consistently good, from Jeep to Ram to the Chrysler Pacifica. A splash of tan leather across the top of the steering wheel matches the seats, and a red panel on the console draws attention to the rocker switch for the terrain modes. Both the Rivian and Jeep feature large touchscreens, but the Recon augments its touchscreen functions with hard buttons (on both the dash and the steering wheel) and knobs for volume and tuning. The Jeep’s Uconnect 5 system also supports wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, while the Rivian doesn’t allow phone mirroring.

Rivian minimizes physical controls in part by aping Tesla’s strategy of forcing scroll wheels into multiple roles. Want to adjust the steering wheel or exterior mirrors? You’ll need to go into a settings menu in the touchscreen and temporarily deputize the steering wheel scroll wheels (“haptic halo wheels,” in Rivian parlance) to handle whichever adjustment you’re pursuing. It’s annoying, but probably not the kind of thing you deal with too often as an owner. At least, while you’re wrestling with that, you can gaze upon the lovely birch trim that spans the dash.

Both interiors allow a view of the sky, with the Rivian employing a fixed panoramic glass roof and the Jeep offering the full convertible experience with its power roll-back soft top. The R2 can also drop its windows (including the back one) with the touch of a button—the rear quarter windows stay fixed, alas. You can remove those in the Recon and, unlike the doors, store them in the car in handy bags. In any case, both SUVs are down with al fresco travel, but the Recon is more committed. The catch is, you’ve got to be committed too.

The Recon and R2 both showcase the hyperbolic performance we’ve quickly come to regard as the EV norm. Why, some of us are old enough to remember when the C5 Corvette Z06’s sub-four-second run to 60 mph was considered wickedly quick. And now we have family off-roaders that will torch that Vette—and plenty of other sports cars besides. To wit: The R2’s dual motors combine for 656 horsepower and 609 pound-feet of torque, good for a 3.5-second 60-mph time and an 11.4-second quarter-mile at 126 mph.

HIGHS: Removable doors and glass, quicker than a Charger Scat Pack, real off-road ability.LOWS: 160 miles of real-world highway range, higher price, Wrangler people will probably leave ducks on it.VERDICT: Jeep’s EV off-roader is fun and fast but far from frugal.

The Jeep is even more powerful, and its huge Nexen Roadian ATX tires are churned by 670 horsepower and 620 pound-feet of torque. The Recon ties the R2 to 60 mph and is slightly behind in the quarter-mile, requiring 11.8 seconds. The Jeep’s quarter-mile time is compromised by its 111-mph speed limiter, which it hits more than a second before it finishes the quarter. And still, it runs 11s. If you’re wondering how quick the Jeep would be minus the doors and glass, superleggera-style, so did we. And we’ll let you know the answer to that next time we get our hands on one.

The Jeep’s 94-kWh battery is bigger than the Rivian’s 88-kWh pack, but the Rivian’s superior efficiency means that it goes longer between charges. In our 75-mph highway range test, the R2 managed 260 miles, a full 100 miles more than the Recon. It also charged a little bit faster, going from 10 to 90 percent charge in 39 minutes, versus 43 minutes for the Jeep. If you’re not doing 75 mph, the Recon fares somewhat better—its EPA-estimated range is 222 miles—but it’s still well short of the 300-mile threshold that’s become a common range expectation for EVs.

Neither the Rivian nor Jeep are particularly impressive dynamically, but as with range, you can divine their handling prowess just by looking at them. On the skidpad, the Jeep holds on for 0.74 g of grip, while the Rivian ekes out 0.81 g. The R2 also out-stops the Recon from 70 mph, 178 feet to 201 feet. We’d guess both those differences would be narrowed if the Rivian wore its available all-terrain tires, but both machines are like old-school muscle cars—hellaciously quick in a straight line but not about to hang with a Mazda Miata in the corners.

Although our two contenders here are calibrated more for on-road comfort than apex-slaying performance, the Recon is far more competent and composed than the Wrangler that it’s cosplaying as—an independent front suspension and rack-and-pinion steering work wonders to modernize the Jeep driving experience. It’s tall, yes, but you don’t get the sense that you’re heaving around in the crow’s nest of an 18th-century schooner, nor does it impart the side-to-side neck snap that presents when overly aggressive anti-roll bars begin asserting themselves. The cushy ride is helped by the all-terrain tires’ generous 70-profile aspect ratio. You won’t likely bend a Recon rim on a pothole or a rock out on the trail.

HIGHS: Stupidly quick, looks great inside and out, the rear glass rolls down!LOWS: Lack of physical controls, light regen setting still too strong, no CarPlay or Android Auto.VERDICT: A premium SUV for the masses that happens to be electric.

Many of us feel the R2 is better to drive than its big sibling, the R1S, despite having a simpler suspension setup with conventional anti-roll bars. The R2 feels like it had plenty of R&D attention, in accordance with its importance to Rivian’s business model. Specifically, the spring and damping rates feel in harmony, with firm body control but enough compliance to soak up nasty pavement. There’s no sense of the suspension abruptly running out of travel, either on droop or compression.

Both the Recon and R2 feature some mandatory brake regeneration when you back off the accelerator, but the Recon’s is milder and feels more like coasting compared to the Rivian’s system. Rivian really wants you to embrace one-pedal driving—in fact, it insists. We’re still not sure why Rivian is so big on mandatory regen, but if you like your car to coast down hills (which, as we’ve explained before, is more efficient than converting kinetic energy to electricity and back again), then the R2 might be a little too one-pedal for you even in its weakest mode.

We didn’t get to really off-road the R2 and Recon, but that contest might be closer than you’d think. The Jeep takes its off-road mission seriously, with 9.1 inches of ground clearance and those 33-inch tires, but the modest Rivian actually has more ground clearance (9.6 inches), and its 32-inch tires aren’t much smaller. Speculatively, they’d both be fun to take muddin’.

The Recon is quick and charismatic, but its high price and stunted range make us think that Jeep built this model as an EV beachhead rather than as a serious volume contender. It’s also better at being a Jeep than it is at being an EV. If you wanted an electric Wrangler, this is the closest thing to it, for now. You can drive it in Mad Max dune-buggy mode, and strangers will leave ducks on the windshield, but the Recon is a fun idea that’s desperately awaiting the next generation of batteries to extend its range. Put it this way: When you’re shelling out more than $70K, it hurts to get smoked on range by the $29,000 Chevy Bolt (262 miles, per the EPA).

So the R2 wins this contest because it delivers the design—and most of the performance—of the R1S at a much lower price point. It’s easy to build a compelling vehicle when you’re charging more than $120,000 (see: the R1S Quad), but it’s much more impressive when you’re targeting the high $60,000 range, the heart of the market. With more than 300 miles of EPA-rated range to go with its scalding acceleration, the R2 is the electric family SUV we’d want to put in our own driveway.

#4311. XBOX CEO Casually Reveals Wolfenstein 3 In Production

Daniel is a lifelong gamer with a love for various genres and gameplay styles who enjoys exploring games and playing from various angles.

The XBOX brand, through its various acquisitions, has managed to obtain ownership of some of the oldest, arguably most important video game IPs. One of those IPs is Wolfenstein, the series that gave us the first true FPS with the release of Wolfenstein 3D all the way back in 1992. Since 2014, the Wolfenstein IP has been in the hands of MachineGames, with Bethesda serving as publisher. Microsoft owns ZeniMax, Zennimax owns Bethesda, and so XBOX usually gets first dibs when Wolfenstein comes knocking.

You might not think it, but a serious shooter like Wolfenstein 3D was a huge influence, according to Randy Pitchford.

It’s rather fitting, then, that someone high up the chain of command in XBOX would have the privilege of divulging new Wolfenstein news. Though, even then, I certainly wouldn’t expect the someone in question to be its literal CEO, nor would I expect said news to drop on a random Thursday, but let nobody say they can’t make things interesting.

On her personal X, formerly Twitter account, XBOX CEO Asha Sharma rather casually announced that MachineGames has officially begun production on the next mainline Wolfenstein game, the first since Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus was released in 2017. Obviously, since production has just started, details are basically non-existent, but both Sharma and MachineGames’ own X account did give us a couple of tidbits to chew on.

Sharma’s tweet keeps the announcement fairly quick and concise, reading, “Wolfenstein 3 is officially in production at @MachineGames. One of gaming's most important franchises, and a team that has done remarkable work bringing it forward. Looking forward to sharing more.”

One of gaming's most important franchises, and a team that has done remarkable work bringing it forward.

Assuming the game will have some manner of subtitle like its predecessors, Sharma didn’t divulge what it was. What she did share, though, was a screenshot of the game’s apparent script. This screenshot is apparently set during the game’s first chapter in a locale called “Nazitraz,” presumably a prison of some sort, in which series protagonist B.J. Blazkowicz confronts a man named “Otto,” who blubbers in fear in his presence. Series mainstay Fergus Reid also appears to be present, but the screenshot cuts off before he says or does anything.

The Elder Scrolls 6 has finally had its title officially confirmed, weeks after it was not so subtly leaked to the wider public.

Shortly after Sharma’s tweet, MachineGames shared the same script screenshot on its own X account alongside the caption, “His reputation precedes him. Wolfenstein 3 is in production.” MachineGames’ post also added a photo of two actors in the midst of motion-capture work: Debra Wilson, who previously played Grace Walker in New Colossus, and B.J.’s actor, Brian Bloom.

Wolfenstein, as a series, has been pretty quiet for a few years now. As I mentioned, New Colossus was the last mainline game to release, which was nearly a decade ago in 2017. The series has had spin-offs since then, including Wolfenstein: Youngblood and Wolfenstein: Cyberpilot, both of which were released in 2019. The former was a co-op game starring B.J.’s teenage daughters as they searched for their father in France, while the latter was a VR game in which an unnamed hacker works to hack various Nazi robots. Unfortunately, neither of these games were particularly well-received.

Still, there’s no reason to be pessimistic, especially considering that it was MachineGames that brought us the unexpected slam dunk that was Indiana Jones and the Great Circle in 2024. I’d say that’s pretty definitive proof that the studio still knows how to put an excellent game together, and I’m optimistic about what’s on the horizon.

Incidentally, MachineGames is also involved in a creative capacity for the live-action Wolfenstein series that’s currently in development for Prime Video. Who knows, we might just have a one-two punch of new Wolfenstein media to look forward to in the not-too-distant future.

MachineGames is making sure the Indiana Jones DLC is challenging, no matter how many hours you've put into the base game.

#4310. Arc Raiders just keeps breaking its own Steam player records

Word of mouth has done wonders for the popularity of Arc Raiders, clearly more than all the pre-launch marketing and hype.

Arc Raiders just cannot be stopped. The extraction shooter from Embark Studios has once again attracted more players over the weekend than it has in its launch week, and over its first weekend on the market.

The positive reception the PvPvE game has garnered from players has clearly caused many of them to convince their friends to jump into this unique gem of a game.

The day Arc Raiders launched, it peaked at 264,673 concurrent players on Steam. Although not massive, it was quite a bit more than the game’s most popular - free - beta test managed to attract.

That figure was broken yet again over the game’s first weekend, with Arc Raiders having reached 354,836 concurrent players on Steam. This is where many thought it would settle, as we start to see the gradual - and expected - decline of player numbers.

To everyone’s surprise, however, Arc Raiders shattered even that record yet again on Sunday, November 9. According to SteamDB, the game peaked at 462,488 concurrent players on Steam, which is a sizeable increase on its launch day numbers. Indeed, should this trend continue, Arc Raiders is going to be well on its way to doubling its initial launch record.

While a few games have broken their launch Steam player records in the past, it’s incredibly rare to see it happen - especially twice in such a short period after launch. Embark clearly has a winner on its hands here.

Arc Raiders’ next big moment is the game’s first post-launch map, which is set to arrive at some point this month, alongside new Quests and other gameplay items. Seeing as how the Steam concurrent record has been broken twice, there’s every chance the arrival of the new map will bring another boost to player numbers.

If you’re among the millions of players who have been exploring the Rust Belt, you’re probably wondering where to find prickly pears, where to find lemons and apricots, and where to find olives - and those links will answer all of those questions. And, if you just jumped in over the weekend, you’re definitely going to find these Arc Raiders tips very helpful.

Acura spruces up its sport compact and celebrates turning 30 with a special edition inspired by one of its most iconic cars.

When Acura revived the Integra nameplate several years ago, it heralded the return of one of the brand’s most iconic models. When the more powerful Type S variant joined the party, Acura could finally offer a true performance-focused car for the first time in years. The new Integra Type S also brought back memories of the legendary DC2 Type R that was sold in America from 1997–2001. For the 2027 model year, Acura is celebrating its 30th anniversary by paying homage to that classic with a new Integra Type S Heritage Edition.

See all results for new 2027 Acura Integra Type S for sale near 94043

Before we get into the details about the Heritage Edition, let’s talk about the changes Acura has made to the standard ‘27 Type S. Every example now features gloss-black 19-inch wheels and mirror caps, and the Brembo-branded brake calipers are now painted yellow. There are no powertrain changes, so a rowdy 320-hp 2.0-liter turbo four and sweet-shifting six-speed manual transmission still feed the front wheels.

Inside, Acura now makes the door-panel trim, door handles, and shift boot dark gray, and that applies to the dashboard too, which also adopts a new diamond pattern. The three knobs that control the climate settings are now all gloss black, and Acura says it has redesigned the upholstery options. The Red and Orchid (white) themes feature faux-suede accents that are black and blue, respectively, but the Ebony option features yellow stitching, which extends to the steering wheel, door panels, and shift boot. The driver’s seat now has memory settings, as does the brake-hold feature, and both exterior mirrors tilt down when the car is put into reverse.

If you missed your chance to buy a Phoenix Yellow Integra Type R back in the day, Acura is turning back the clock and giving you another shot. Sure, the new Type S model has an extra pair of doors and put on some weight, but it remains one of our favorite driver’s cars, and the Heritage Edition is the only way to get the new Blazing Phoenix Yellow paint job (at least for the ‘27 model year). Not only is the new retro-themed Type S the first Integra with yellow paint since the 2001 Type R, but it also features exclusive copper-colored wheels. Its interior color is limited to the black-and-yellow theme offered on other new Type S models, but the Heritage Edition alone has a titanium shift knob—same as the Honda Civic Type R.

See all results for new 2027 Acura Integra Type S for sale near 94043

Acura says the 2027 versions of the Integra Type S will reach dealerships sometime next month. While that includes the new Heritage Edition, it’s limited to just 700 examples for U.S. audiences. For those who are lucky enough to score one, it’s only $2300 more than the regular Type S, which starts at $55,995.

#4308. Battlefield 6 patch finally ends the menace of the Lock-Guided Missile, shuts down the Recon Drone Sledgehammer exploit and more

Today's Battlefield 6 patch is laser-focused on taking care of some of the more infuriating bugs while also taking out a couple of exploits.

The next Battlefield 6 update is here. Having gone live just moments ago, update 1.1.1.5 is something of a midseason update, bringing a few quality of life tweaks to the game alongside some key fixes for a few of the issues that cropped up since the launch of Season 1 in late October.

This latest release is also the first to tackle some of the problems players have been running into playing Redsec battle royale, the free-to-play component that also came out recently.

Patch 1.1.1.5 is fairly limited in scope. The biggest fix in this one comes to the Lock-Guided Missiles going through flares, and generally being annoying enough to stop players from using air vehicles altogether.

The Lock-Guided Missiles were mainly used by AA vehicles, but they could also be equipped by IFVs, which made it even more of a nightmare to pilots. It got so bad that Battlefield Studios disabled it entirely while the team worked on a proper fix.

Another exploit the patch fixes is the one that allowed players to stand on the Recon Drone and reach areas they’re not supposed to. This was done by… repeatedly hitting it with a Sledgehammer. The long-running issue of vehicles not spawning for certain teams in Conquest and Breakthrough appears to have finally been fixed, too.

In terms of battle royale, the patch has a few fixes that should help make the experience more consistent, as well as improve the flow of matches. One of the more interesting addresses an issue that could eliminate the entire squad instead of reviving dead teammates when using a Mobile Spawn.

Patch 1.1.1.5 also has yet more adjustments to weapon dispersion (bloom). Some of the casses it addresses include transitioning from sprint to firing in ADS, and others where it apparently scaled with player movement speed.

#4307. Rimac Is Reportedly Ending Nevera Production After Selling Just 71 Cars

The electric hypercar set plenty of records, but it may have come in well under the purportedly planned production run of 190 examples.

Rimac is ending production of its all-electric Nevera hypercar at the end of 2026, Germany’s Auto Motor und Sport reports. And somewhat surprisingly, the same report suggests that just 71 of 190 planned Reveras were built over the course of its production run.

The base Nevera, and its later Nevera R variant, have held a number of records, including the title of world’s quickest car, what was once the EV lap record at the Nürburgring Nordschleife, and a quarter-mile run under 7.9 seconds. Those numbers may not have been enough to make the model a hit with buyers, though. According to the report, 51 of a planned 150 base-model Neveras were built, and 20 out of a planned 40 Nevera Rs reached production.

While the apparent final tally of Nevera production is striking, it is part of a larger pattern of electric hypercars failing to find an audience. The Lotus Evija once competed directly with Rimac’s Nevera, but Lotus has since moved on to a hybrid supercar with V-8 power. Former Rimac stakeholder Porsche once considered its own electric hypercar, only to pivot to an internal-combustion supercar instead. Even as cars like the Tesla Roadster and Yangwang U9 Xtreme make headlines with record-setting stunts, there are questions on whether or not a conventional hypercar buyer would be interested in paying for an EV.

See all results for Rimac Nevera for sale near 33463

Whether or not the Nevera itself was a success, the halo car did succeed in raising Rimac’s profile. Namesake founder Mate Rimac is now fully in charge of Bugatti, and Rimac Technology provides electric powertrain components to major cars like the Porsche 911 Turbo S. As the most significant electric hypercar to reach the market to date—well, perhaps along with the closely related Pininfarina Battista—the few Neveras in private hands represent a major leap forward for both electric performance and the Rimac brand itself.

Fred Smith's love of cars comes from his fascination with auto racing. Unfortunately, that passion led him to daily drive a high-mileage, first-year Porsche Panamera. He is still thinking about the last lap of the 2011 Indianapolis 500.

#4306. Arc Raiders has proven that extraction shooters can be popular, with over 4 million copies sold in under two weeks

Arc Raiders has sold even more copies, which we should've guessed, given that the game keeps breaking its own concurrent player records.

It’s pretty clear at this stage that Arc Raiders is one of the biggest launches of 2025. More interesting than the numbers themselves, however, is that this is an extraction shooter - a subgenre which has typically been thought of as niche.

If you’ve been paying the PvPvE game any attention, you could easily see how (and why) it keeps breaking its own records.

Today, publisher Nexon announced in a press release (via Gematsu) that Arc Raiders has now sold over 4 million copies. The game came out on October 30, which means it managed to sell that many copies in a little over 10 days.

The news comes on the same day that developer Embark Studios announced that the game had more than 700,000 concurrent players across all platforms over the weekend. Over the same weekend on Steam alone, Arc Raiders broke its own Steam concurrent record with a new peak of 462,488 players - which is a significant chunk of that 700,000+ player base.

This marks the second time the extraction shooter has broken its own concurrent player records, which is something very few games have managed in the past. Arc Raiders remains a top-seller, too. On Steam, it’s currently the second-best seller globally (by revenue), sitting just below Counter-Strike 2.

“The many different ways you play and participate in ARC Raiders have completely blown us away, going far beyond what we ever imagined. You surprise us, you outsmart us, and you keep us on our toes. We wouldn’t have it any other way,” the developer wrote on Twitter.

Embark recently published a roadmap to highlight all the new content coming to the game over the remainder of this year. The first new map is set to arrive this month alongside new Arc units, new gameplay items, new events and more.

Just over the weekend, the game received several new Map Conditions that completely alter the way they play. The developer has already rolled out a couple of updates since launch, in order to tackle exploits and fix a few launchday bugs.

If you’re currently hooked on this gem of a game, we guarantee that our Arc Raiders gameplay tips will have at least one you didn’t know about. We also have more guides on how to find some of the more elusive items in the game, such as olives, lemons and apricots, and prickly pears.

#4304. Arc Raiders' new map will be unlocked through a community event that starts today, and everyone has to donate

It looks like it's going to take the Arc Raiders community a bit of work to unlock the game's next map.

As many of Arc Raiders’ regular players predicted, the game’s first post-launch map won’t just be available for everyone, it will instead be closely tied to a community event. Breaking New Ground is the name of that event, and it’s one where everyone will need to contribute in order to rebuild some old tunnels and unlock the way to Stella Montis.

The event kicks off today alongside the release of the game’s latest patch. The ask is relatively simple: players must commit Basic Materials to the project so that the tunnels can be rebuilt. This option will be available to anyone who’s played at least five rounds.

If you’ve spent any time in Arc Raiders, you’ll know that Basic Materials are things like Metal parts, Fabric, Chemicals, Rubber Parts, and Plastic Parts - most of which are easy to find in the game’s various maps.

Even beyond the ultimate goal of unlocking the new map, donations will also reward you with Merits, which is a new event currency, though there’s a cap on how many you can earn.

Once enough materials have been collected, the next phase of the event, Staking Our Claim, will begin, which will bring a new progression track to the game, and make Stella Montis available for players to visit.

Developer Embark describes the new environment as unlike any that we have seen in the game so far. It’s a facility carved into the northern mountains, which means it’s going to have a near-pristine look; quite the contrast with the rest of the game’s environments.

Stella Montis also has its own Arc enemies, loot, schematics, and other gameplay items. You can look forward to coming across the Shredder, a close-quarter Arc unit exclusive to the new map for now.

Then there’s The Matriarch, a somehow even larger version of the Queen. Thankfully, it will only be available under a specific map condition, so you’re in no danger of running into her randomly. The update will also introduce a new legendary weapon, two new grenades, and three new mines.

Staking Our Claim will only run until December, which is when the next stage of the game’s roadmap will kick off. Then, the Cold Snap update will introduce the Flickering Flames event, the first snowfall Map Condition, and the Expedition Project voluntary wipe.
